name: Preventing Malaria in Your Family
objectives: Given your own household, explain how malaria spreads and list who in your home is most at risk, naming the mosquito bite at night and naming young children and pregnant women

Given a treated bed net and the places your family sleeps, hang a treated net, tuck it in and repair any holes, with every person, starting with young children and pregnant women, sleeping under a net every night
Given the area around your home, remove or cover the places where mosquitoes breed and block their way into the house, carrying out at least three actions in one week

Given a pregnant woman or a young child in your family, list the malaria services your clinic offers them and plan the visits, naming early antenatal visits and asking about vaccines and preventive medicine where offered

Given a family member with a fever in a malaria area, take the person for a malaria test the same day and follow the health worker's treatment, never treating with leftover or unknown medicine and never stopping early
Given a sick family member, spot the danger signs of severe malaria and take the person to the clinic at once, naming at least four danger signs and the nearest clinic or community health worker

lessons.title: Lesson 1: How malaria spreads and who is most at risk
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain how malaria spreads and list who in your home is most at risk.
This lesson builds toward: Given your own household, you will explain how malaria spreads and list who in your home is most at risk, naming the mosquito bite at night and naming young children and pregnant women.
Malaria is caused by a tiny parasite. It is spread by the bite of certain female mosquitoes (Anopheles). A mosquito bites a person with malaria, then bites someone else and passes it on. It does not pass directly from person to person by touch, food or air.
These mosquitoes bite mostly in the late evening and at night, often while people sleep. Signs of malaria usually start 10 to 15 days after the bite, with fever, chills and headache.
WHO says those most at risk of severe malaria are babies and children under 5, pregnant women, people with HIV, and travellers who come from places without malaria. In Africa, most malaria deaths are young children. WHO reports that Nigeria and DR Congo alone had over 40% of the region's malaria deaths in 2024. In much of North Africa local malaria is rare, but people from Morocco, Egypt or Tunisia who travel to malaria areas are at high risk and should see a health worker before they go.
Words to know:
- Parasite: a tiny living thing that lives in another body and harms it.
- Anopheles: the kind of mosquito that spreads malaria.
- At risk: more likely to get sick or very sick.
Official sources:
- World Health Organization: Malaria fact sheet (spread, symptoms, danger signs, nets, spraying, chemoprevention, vaccines, testing)
- CDC: About malaria (bites in the late evening and at night, symptoms, seek care quickly)
Try it now: Write the names of everyone who sleeps in your home. Circle those most at risk: children under 5, any pregnant woman, anyone with HIV, and visitors from places without malaria.
You can now explain how malaria spreads and say who in your home is most at risk.

options: Through the bite of certain mosquitoes
check.why: Malaria is passed by the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes, not by touch, food or weather.

check.q: Who in a family is most at risk of severe malaria?
options: Young children under 5 and pregnant women
check.why: WHO names young children and pregnant women among those most at risk.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: A treated net every night
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Hang a treated bed net, tuck it in and repair any holes.
This lesson builds toward: Given a treated bed net and the places your family sleeps, you will hang a treated net, tuck it in and repair any holes, with every person, starting with young children and pregnant women, sleeping under a net every night.
A bed net treated with insecticide (often called an ITN or a long-lasting net) is one of the main ways WHO recommends to prevent malaria. The net stops mosquitoes reaching you while you sleep, and the insecticide kills or weakens those that land on it. WHO says newer types of nets protect better where mosquitoes no longer die from the old insecticide.
A net only works when it is used every night, all year, not just in the rainy season. Hang it over the bed or sleeping mat so it reaches the floor, tuck the edges under the mattress or mat before dark, and get in without leaving gaps. If there are not enough nets for everyone, young children and pregnant women sleep under one first, then work to get nets for the rest.
Look after it: check for holes every week and sew or knot them closed straight away. Wash it gently and not too often, and dry it in the shade, following the instructions on the packet or from your health worker. Do not use nets for fishing, fencing or gardens. Many national programmes give nets free at clinics, antenatal visits, schools or in campaigns: ask your clinic or community health worker.
Step by step:
- Hang the net over the bed or mat so it reaches the floor.
- Tuck the edges under the mattress or mat before dark.
- Get in without leaving gaps, every night.
- Check for holes every week and close them at once.
- Wash gently, not too often, and dry it in the shade.
- Ask your clinic or community health worker about free nets.
Words to know:
- Insecticide: a chemical that kills insects.
- ITN (insecticide-treated net): a bed net treated with insecticide to keep off and kill mosquitoes.
- Campaign: a time when health workers give out nets or services to many people.
Official sources:
- World Health Organization: Malaria fact sheet (spread, symptoms, danger signs, nets, spraying, chemoprevention, vaccines, testing)
Try it now: Tonight, check every net in your home. Hang each one so it reaches the floor, tuck it in and close any holes. Count how many more nets your family needs.
You can now hang, tuck in and care for a treated net so everyone, starting with the most at risk, sleeps under one every night.

check.q: When should your family sleep under the net?
check.why: Mosquitoes can bite and spread malaria all year; the net works only when used every night.

check.q: You find a small hole in the net. What do you do?
options: Wait until the hole is bigger
Sew or knot it closed straight away
check.why: Mosquitoes get through small holes; closing them at once keeps the net working.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Fewer mosquitoes and fewer bites around the home
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Remove or cover the places where mosquitoes breed and block their way into the house.
This lesson builds toward: Given the area around your home, you will remove or cover the places where mosquitoes breed and block their way into the house, carrying out at least three actions in one week.
Mosquitoes lay their eggs in still water. Puddles, old tyres, tins, broken pots, blocked drains, uncovered water drums and buckets can all become breeding places close to where your family sleeps.
Around the home: empty or turn over things that hold water; cover water drums, buckets and tanks with a lid or a tight cloth; clear blocked gutters and drains; fill puddles with soil. Do this every week, especially in the rainy season, and work with neighbours, because mosquitoes fly between houses.
Keep them out and avoid bites: close doors and windows at dusk and fix screens on windows and eaves if you can. In the evening, wear long sleeves and long trousers or a long wrapper. Repellents with DEET, IR3535 or icaridin can help after dusk; use them as the label says. Coils and vaporizers can help too, but never replace the net. If spray teams from the health programme come to spray inside homes (indoor residual spraying), let them in and follow their advice about not washing or painting the walls afterwards.
Step by step:
- Walk around your home and find everything that holds still water.
- Empty, turn over, cover or remove it.
- Clear blocked drains and fill puddles.
- Close doors and windows at dusk; fix screens if you can.
- Cover arms and legs in the evening; use repellent as the label says.
- Let the health programme's spray teams in.
Words to know:
- Breeding place: still water where mosquitoes lay eggs.
- Repellent: a cream or spray that keeps mosquitoes off your skin.
- Indoor residual spraying (IRS): health workers spraying insecticide on inside walls to kill mosquitoes that rest there.
Official sources:
- World Health Organization: Malaria fact sheet (spread, symptoms, danger signs, nets, spraying, chemoprevention, vaccines, testing)
- World Health Organization: Drinking-water fact sheet (household water containers as mosquito breeding sites; cover them)
Try it now: Walk around your home now. Write every place with still water. Empty, cover or remove at least three today, and plan to check again every week.
You can now remove mosquito breeding places around your home and cut down bites in the evening.

check.q: Where do mosquitoes lay their eggs?
options: In still water like puddles, tyres and open buckets
check.why: Mosquitoes need still water to lay their eggs.

check.q: You use a mosquito coil in the evening. What is true?
options: It can help, but you still sleep under a net
You no longer need a net
It must burn all night next to the baby
check.why: Coils and repellents add protection but never replace the net.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Protecting the most at risk and acting fast

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Protecting pregnant women and young children
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the malaria services your clinic offers pregnant women and young children and plan the visits.
This lesson builds toward: Given a pregnant woman or a young child in your family, you will list the malaria services your clinic offers them and plan the visits, naming early antenatal visits and asking about vaccines and preventive medicine where offered.
Malaria in pregnancy can harm both the mother and the baby: WHO says it can cause the baby to be born too early or too small. A pregnant woman should start antenatal visits early and go to every one. At antenatal care in many countries she can get a treated net, malaria testing and, where the national programme offers it, preventive medicine for malaria in pregnancy (WHO calls this IPTp). The health worker decides what she needs and when. Never take malaria medicine in pregnancy without a health worker.
For young children: WHO recommends two malaria vaccines (RTS,S and R21) for children in areas with a lot of malaria, and they are being added to routine child vaccinations in many African countries. In some areas, for example parts of the Sahel such as Burkina Faso and Mali, health workers also give young children preventive medicine during the rainy season (seasonal malaria chemoprevention). Ask your clinic what is offered where you live and keep the child's health card up to date.
Vaccines and preventive medicine add protection, but WHO says they work best together with nets. Keep using the net every night. Write the clinic dates in your plan, and ask your community health worker if you cannot get to the clinic.
Step by step:
- Pregnant woman: start antenatal visits early and go to every one.
- Ask at antenatal care about a net, testing and preventive medicine for malaria.
- Child: ask the clinic whether malaria vaccines are given where you live and keep the health card up to date.
- Ask if there are rainy-season preventive medicine campaigns in your area.
- Write every clinic date in your plan and keep using nets.
Words to know:
- Antenatal care: health check-ups for a woman during pregnancy.
- Vaccine: a medicine, usually an injection, that helps the body protect itself from a disease.
- Preventive medicine: medicine a health worker gives to stop an illness before it starts.
- Health card: the card or booklet where the clinic records a child's vaccines and check-ups.
Official sources:
- World Health Organization: Malaria fact sheet (spread, symptoms, danger signs, nets, spraying, chemoprevention, vaccines, testing)
Try it now: If anyone in your home is pregnant or under 5, write down the next clinic date for each and the questions you will ask about nets, vaccines and preventive medicine. If no one is, write it for a neighbour or relative you can help.
You can now name the clinic services that protect pregnant women and young children from malaria and plan the visits.

check.q: A woman in your family is pregnant. What is the first step to protect her from malaria?
options: Buy malaria medicine at the market
Start antenatal visits early, sleep under a net and ask about malaria protection
check.why: Early antenatal care plus a net gives her the protection the clinic offers.

check.q: Your child had the malaria vaccine. What about the net?
options: Only use it in the rainy season
Keep using it every night; vaccines work best with nets
check.why: WHO says vaccines give the most benefit combined with nets and other measures.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Fever: get a test the same day
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Take a family member with a fever for a malaria test the same day.
This lesson builds toward: Given a family member with a fever in a malaria area, you will take the person for a malaria test the same day and follow the health worker's treatment, never treating with leftover or unknown medicine and never stopping early.
In a malaria area, treat every fever as possible malaria until a test says otherwise. Malaria often starts like many other illnesses, with fever, chills, headache and body aches, so you cannot tell by looking. WHO recommends that every suspected case is confirmed with a test, a rapid diagnostic test or a microscope, before treatment.
Go the same day to a clinic, health centre or trained community health worker who can test. A rapid test takes a drop of blood from a finger and gives a result in minutes. In a child under 5, a fever should never wait until tomorrow.
If the test shows malaria, the health worker chooses the medicine and tells you how to take it. Take all of it, exactly as told, even if the person feels better. Do not use leftover medicine, medicine meant for someone else, or unknown medicine from a market or hawker: it may be the wrong type, too little or fake. If the test is negative, the health worker looks for another cause. If the person is not better, or gets worse, go back.
Step by step:
- Fever in a malaria area? Treat it as possible malaria.
- Go the same day to a clinic or a community health worker who can test.
- If malaria is found: take the medicine exactly as the health worker says, all of it.
- Never use leftover, borrowed or unknown medicine.
- Not better or worse? Go back at once.
Words to know:
- Rapid diagnostic test (RDT): a quick test with a drop of blood from a finger that shows malaria in minutes.
- Negative result: the test did not find malaria.
- Fake medicine: medicine that looks real but has the wrong amount or nothing that works.
Official sources:
- World Health Organization: Malaria fact sheet (spread, symptoms, danger signs, nets, spraying, chemoprevention, vaccines, testing)
- CDC: About malaria (bites in the late evening and at night, symptoms, seek care quickly)
Try it now: Find out where your family can get a malaria test the same day: the nearest clinic or community health worker, the opening hours, and how you would get there. Write it in your plan.
You can now get every fever tested the same day and follow only the health worker's treatment, all of it.

check.q: Your child has a fever in the evening. What do you do?
options: Get a malaria test the same day from a clinic or community health worker
Give leftover medicine from last time
check.why: WHO advises testing before treatment, and a child's fever should not wait.

check.q: After two days of malaria medicine, your husband feels better. What should he do?
options: Stop and keep the rest for next time
Finish all of it exactly as the health worker said
Give the rest to a neighbour
check.why: Stopping early can let the malaria come back; take it all as told.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Danger signs of severe malaria and your family plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot the danger signs of severe malaria and get the person to a clinic at once.
This lesson builds toward: Given a sick family member, you will spot the danger signs of severe malaria and take the person to the clinic at once, naming at least four danger signs and the nearest clinic or community health worker.
Malaria can become severe quickly, especially in young children and pregnant women. Severe malaria is an emergency.
WHO lists these danger signs. Go to the clinic or hospital NOW, day or night, if the person: is extremely tired or weak, or cannot sit or stand; is confused, very sleepy or hard to wake; has fits (convulsions), especially more than once; has difficulty breathing; has dark or bloody urine; has yellow eyes or skin; or has unusual bleeding. A child who cannot drink or breastfeed, or who vomits everything, also needs the clinic now.
Be ready before it happens: write the danger signs and the name, place and phone number of your nearest clinic, hospital and community health worker on a card on the wall; know how you will get there at night; and keep some transport money aside if you can. Then put everything from this course into your household malaria plan.
Step by step:
- Learn the danger signs.
- If you see any: go to the clinic or hospital now, day or night.
- Make a card with the signs and your nearest clinic's and health worker's names and numbers.
- Plan how you will travel at night and keep transport money if you can.
- Write your household malaria plan.
Words to know:
- Severe malaria: malaria that has become dangerous to life and needs a hospital or clinic at once.
- Convulsions (fits): sudden shaking of the body that the person cannot control.
- Jaundice: yellow colour in the eyes or skin.
Official sources:
- World Health Organization: Malaria fact sheet (spread, symptoms, danger signs, nets, spraying, chemoprevention, vaccines, testing)
Try it now: Make your danger-signs card now with at least four signs and your nearest clinic's or community health worker's name and number. Then write your full household malaria plan from the final task.
You can now spot the danger signs of severe malaria, get help at once, and keep a household malaria plan.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Who is at risk No one is marked as most at risk, or the plan does not say how malaria spreads. Young children, pregnant women and other high-risk people in the home are named, with the night mosquito bite as the cause. Also plans for visitors or travellers from places without malaria. Nets every night Nets are counted but not who sleeps under them, or holes are not mentioned. Every sleeping place is listed with a net, the most at risk first, with weekly hole checks and gentle care. Missing nets are counted and the learner has asked the clinic or community health worker how to get them. Fewer mosquitoes Fewer than three actions, or actions that do not remove still water or block bites. At least three actions, such as emptying containers, covering drums, clearing drains and closing doors at dusk. A weekly check day is set and neighbours are involved. Clinic services No clinic visits planned for a pregnant woman or young child in the home. Antenatal visits and child clinic dates are written, with questions about nets, vaccines and preventive medicine. Visits are booked or done, and the child's health card is up to date. Fever action The plan includes home treatment with leftover or market medicine, or waiting to see. A same-day test at a named clinic or community health worker, and the full treatment as the health worker says. Opening hours and a back-up place to test are written too. Danger-signs card Fewer than four danger signs, or no clinic contact. At least four danger signs and the nearest clinic's or health worker's name and number. Also a night transport plan, with no medicine names or doses on the card. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: A child with malaria starts having fits. What do you do?
options: Wait to see if it stops
Give more of the same medicine
Go to the clinic or hospital now
Let the child sleep it off
check.why: Convulsions are a danger sign of severe malaria; it is an emergency.

check.q: Which is a danger sign of severe malaria?
options: Feeling a bit hot after work
Yellow eyes, or dark or bloody urine
check.why: WHO lists jaundice and dark or bloody urine as danger signs that need emergency care.
